The law should be updated, therefore, to make clear that gig economy workers are employees entitled to the full range of legal protections and benefits afforded to other workers. The labor movement has a long history of fighting for working people and those who aspire to join the middle class by ensuring they can bargain collectively for better wages and working conditions. That fight is far from over, given the existence of so-called “Right-to-Work” legislation in 28 states and localities. This legislation undermines the ability of unions to effectively advocate for their members in the workplace. And it does so by eliminating requirements to pay union dues for workers who enjoy all benefits without paying any costs of obtaining them. It is time to update labor laws with an expansion of collective bargaining rights for all workers, including those in the public sector. It’s time we modernize our laws so that a higher minimum wage is enforced at both state and national levels. When more people have money in their pockets and can afford basic necessities, they are more likely to spend it on goods or services from local businesses — boosting our economy overall. But a few firms are shamelessly exploiting the coronavirus crisis to delay and undermine workers’ rights. Allowing app-based delivery companies to flout these rights in the midst of this crisis would be both unfair and unconscionable. Delivery firms such as Deliveroo have sought to argue that they are not “employers” and should therefore be exempt from these rules. They are misleading the public. The legal framework is clear: in the UK, as in other EU countries, app-platform delivery businesses such as Uber Eats and Deliveroos are defined as “employment businesses”. To argue otherwise is a question of semantics, because for five years we have all worked under the assumption that they were employment businesses under existing legal definitions. They cannot change this now for their own convenience. During the Covid-19 pandemic, these firms have been helping many people by delivering food and other goods to their doors. We should thank them for their efforts during difficult times – but we should not allow them to cheat their way out of providing hardworking couriers with decent pay and conditions at this time or any time. That means a minimum wage, the right to collective bargaining, the ability to join a union and more. We must also ensure that new technology does not deepen the divides in our society or reduce the quality of work for those who undertake it. As we stand on the cusp of a new industrial revolution, we should not shun these changes. But we must shape them so they benefit everyone, not just a privileged few. That is why I can today announce that when we implement our manifesto commitment to strengthen employment rights for all workers, we will legislate for a new right that will protect anyone doing this kind of work. If they are wrongly denied basic employment rights such as holiday pay or sick leave, they will be able to take their employer to court and seek redress. And if they successfully win their case, I can confirm that employers who refuse to pay up will face fines of up to 200 per cent of whatever sum is owed. This reform ensures that no one working in the gig economy is treated as disposable; it protects people against unscrupulous bosses who treat them as nothing more than an expendable pair of hands; and it sends out a clear message: if you work hard and do your job you should be rewarded fairly in return. These changes are long overdue but this Conservative Government will finally make them happen and we will do so in our first 100 days in office .

prompt_text: A country's sovereign debt should be restructured when repayment requires severe cuts to essential public services.
responses: The IMF has called for an overhaul of sovereign debt workouts, but to date it has not been implemented. Debt restructuring is needed when a country faces a debt service burden that requires austerity so severe that it risks undermining the recovery of the economy and thereby preventing a return to growth. Austerity in this context does not necessarily mean cutting government spending on goods and services, but could also mean having to increase taxes or cut back on investment, both of which are likely to slow the economy. This kind of austeritarian policy is often backed by the IMF with financial support from donor countries such as Germany and France. The adverse impact on growth of some past bailout programs run by the Fund have been widely documented." For example, IMF-backed austerarian policies in Greece and Argentina caused economic damage far greater than the initial shocks that justified such policies. When Sri Lanka went bankrupt in 1989 and was granted debt relief by its creditors, including commercial banks, international agencies and governments, it agreed to structural adjustment policies as part of the deal. The first phase contained many reforms that could be welcomed by all, including freeing prices, removing restrictions on imports, privatizing state enterprises etc. But these measures did not restructure the economy adequately; they simply shifted wealth from one group to another within society ("structural readjustment without fundamental restructuration").

There are alternatives to austerity and to the IMF and their erratic and harsh policies. The UK government spent more than it received in tax revenue and its national debt spiralled out of control. By 10 February 2008, the UK’s total government debt including financial liabilities was £537.5 billion (about £464 billion in today's money) or 46% of GDP. prompt_text: Laws against hate speech are a necessary protection for vulnerable groups and do not constitute an unacceptable restriction on free expression.
responses: However, some laws in Europe abridge legitimate free speech and are not based on international standards. European countries must ensure that punishments for hate speech are proportionate to their offensiveness and not disproportionate. Countries must also ensure that the law is not used to punish those who do not use hateful language, but rather express opinions that are only criticised as such by those who disagree with them. In Sweden, for example, an academic was earlier charged with hate speech for saying that men have shorter life expectancies than women because they commit more suicide. This was interpreted as "hate against men". Such prosecutions show the need to ensure that laws against hate speech do not violate freedom of expression. We need stronger European Fundamental Rights protection through the Charter of Fundamentals Rights and the restriction of limitations to those that are "necessary and proportionate". This is the judgment of the European Court of Human Rights in a decision on Austria this week. The complaint was brought by an Austrian nationalist who was fined by an appeals court for hate speech. The ruling means that many of the restrictions on free expression in Europe are lawful. The complainant, Norbert Hofer, was convicted under Article 283 of the Austrian Criminal Code for his statements that migrants were “animals” and “cancer” and should be gassed, for provoking violence against asylum seekers and for suggesting that migrant women should be raped. He argued that his statements were not intended to cause harm and therefore did not constitute hate speech within the meaning of Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which is incorporated into Article 7 of Austria’s constitution. He took his case to the court claiming that he had been persecuted for expressing opinions against mass migration. The government argued that Article 4(2) of the ICCPR, which allows restrictions on freedom of expression where necessary for respecting rights or reputation of others, applies to hate speech because it constitutes a form of harassment against certain groups based on their identity or membership in particular communities. Any restriction on free expression must be necessary and proportionate. It is not necessary to criminalise every instance of offensive speech as a matter of course. The Government will consult fully before enacting any legislation. The prosecution of hate crimes should be seen as a means of providing justice rather than as a form of censorship. Hate crimes are a blight on our communities and undermine the sense of security on which civilised society depends. In order to deal with hate crime effectively, we need more than legislation. We need to change attitudes and perceptions, and we must make sure that there is no safe haven for those who would incite hatred and prejudice against others. Now more than ever, our communities need confidence in the police service, and the whole criminal justice system needs to work to ensure that the victims of these crimes feel safe enough to report them in the first place, confident that they will be taken seriously by police officers when they do so, and able to trust that their cases will be dealt with swiftly by the courts with justice and fairness. It demonstrates the Government's commitment to stamping out hate crime and all forms of racism in our society that we have given nearly £17 million in recent years towards tackling those issues through improving community policing, supporting awareness-raising campaigns, such as Tell Mama-the Measuring Anti-Muslim Attacks project-and working with groups such as Community Security Trust to keep vulnerable people safe.

However, the definition of hate speech and its practical application must be carefully formulated so that it is based on reason. Excessive and unreasonable definitions can be used to limit freedom of expression in a way that violates Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). While an international convention does not allow for any interpretation in Italy, it is worth looking at how various European countries have dealt with this issue. Hate speech can take two forms: incitement to and justification of violence/hatred towards individuals or groups on the basis of their membership of a protected category (e.g. race, religion, gender, sexual orientation). The first form is most commonly used and has been extensively analysed by the European Court of Human Rights based on Article 7 of the ECHR. In recent years, however, a new trend has emerged: inciting hatred against individuals or categories because they are considered morally inferior to others. This latter approach has led to more frequent lawsuits against institutions such as The Church Of Scientology International and other religious organisations, as well as towards people who have expressed opinions considered offensive by some members within society. Consequently, we must ask ourselves what constitutes ‘hate speech’ under different definitions around Europe-and how these definitions are applied in practice-in order to make sure they do not unjustifiably restrict free expression while protecting vulnerable groups from hateful speech that risks leading them into

The originally proposed penalty of up to seven years in prison was reduced in 2003 to a maximum of two years. That is still excessive, and any threat of imprisonment should be used only as a last resort. There are alternatives to criminal prosecution for people who cross the line into hate speech: the law already allows for civil proceedings and out-of-court resolutions. More use should be made of these mechanisms where appropriate. As well as ensuring that the law is applied proportionately, we must also make sure that its scope is clear and its language sufficiently defined. For example, what constitutes “insulting” behaviour? It is also noteworthy that court cases are becoming fewer and that there has been no major change in the way this legislation has been applied during the last decade. Concern about overzeal has been muted compared with other proposals relating to free expression which are now before parliament: a plan for a European hate crime directive which would set severe penalties for verbal abuse; and proposals for an internet blocking order which would enable private litigants to secure an injunction against publication on the World Wide Web before an offence has even occurred. Governments should ensure that hate speech laws are formulated with care and precision and are not overbroad. They should also respect their obligation to protect public expression, including when it occurs in the private sphere. In particular, their obligation under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights – the right for individuals to express themselves freely – covers all forum of expression, whether it be public or private, Print, broadcasting or digital. This broad interpretation includes social platforms and provides protection to those who wish to express their views online. Public authorities are responsible for protecting free expression as well as vulnerable communities – they must enforce hate speech legislation with care while upholding free expression. They must be aware of the struggles faced by minority communities and how these struggles relate to freedom of expression. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly upheld restrictions on hate speech and the United Nations Human Rights Committee has stated that “the scope of article 19 [of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the human rights treaty] does not authorize advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence.” As a result, laws restricting hate speech are common in Europe and the world. Restrictions on hateful speech are not only common internationally but also necessary to prevent vulnerable groups from being harmed by propaganda designed to instill hatred and fear. Laws against hate speech provide a way for those who are vulnerable to speak up against those who would propagandize against them. prompt_text: Governments should not have access to citizens' encrypted communications under any circumstances.
responses: That is the simple conclusion from a recent paper published by the Centre for Data, Governance and Society at Leeds University, which is entitled "Outlawing Encryption: A Discussion of Justifications and Consequences". The paper, written by Professor Ross Anderson and Dr Markus Kuhn of the university and Dr Neil Thompson of King's College London, is a timely addition to this debate. It shows how concerns over encryption should be seen as part of a wider problem about governments' attempts to use technology to increase their power over citizens. The paper outlines some of the many ways in which such attempts have been made. Often they are made under the banner of preventing terrorism or crime. However, as the authors note, that is largely misleading. "The control of communications technologies is primarily used to combat political dissent rather than criminality," they argue. "In particular, widespread use of GSM [global system for mobile communications] allows governments to deal with dissidents far more effectively than predecessor technologies." Other examples are provided, including not only China's use of facial recognition technology but also Australia's attempt to force telcos to store metadata on every Australian for two years; New Zealand's Cybersecurity Act and its own GCSB (government communications security bureau) Bill; and Canada's Bill C-30 (Protecting Communities and Improving Public Safety Act). All those initiatives have come under fire during

When law enforcement agencies are unable to access encrypted communications they must resort to other means of surveillance. Laws that allow backdoors in encryption will only lead to further erosion of privacy rights. The call for a right to “read, write and participate” in the networked world opens the door for the freedom of expression and association, which are protected under human rights law. Internet governance principles should be based on national and international human rights laws and norms. With regard to cybersecurity, it is important to note that security is a function of the broader society’s ability to detect, prevent, and respond to threats. Most threats will not come from within the system but from actors outside of it. It is therefore important to cultivate pluralism in this context as well. Governments should not make false promises of security if citizens refuse to give up their right to privacy or be subjected to censorship. Classical liberals believe that government action should be limited to cases that cannot be determined by individuals or markets. For much of the 20th century, there was a robust debate among conservatives over whether international trade should be left to free markets or regulated by government. The proponents of regulation were known as mercantilists: followers of the political economist and statesman Adam Smith, who believed that international trade can damage domestic economic development. They include a range of conservative thinkers, from Abraham Lincoln to Milton Friedman, who warned of the consequences of unrestrained trade with China. By contrast, the proponents for leaving international trade to free market forces are neoliberals, or neocons, who advocate for unsustainably opening up world markets to international competition. Notable neocoms include Milton Freidman and his apprentice George W. Bush. How should governments balance strong border controls with a competitive economy. Many economists believe that the welfare of their nation, and the world, would be enhanced by making markets for goods and services more open to global competition. Free trade, they argue, would allow countries to specialize in the products and services at which they excel; consumers would enjoy greater choice and lower prices; and all would benefit from increasing efficiency and productivity. The opposing economic case is that trade liberalization would cause severe unemployment in "sensitive" sectors such as manufacturing-based industries. The political case against free trade is that it threatens workers' jobs, wages, and working conditions, undermines government attempts to secure social justice (particularly with respect to trade unions), endangers national security through the loss of strategic industries, cuts taxes by reducing government revenues (as tariffs fall), and skews the balance of payments towards a deficit which must be financed by overseas lending. Above all, free trade threatens the nation's sovereignty by subjecting its democratic government to foreign competition. Therefore national governments must retain some public control over their borders in order to protect their workers from being undercut by cheap foreign labor and firms from being driven out of business by foreign competitors. The word was first used in the 5th century BC by Athenians to describe the power of the common people. The notion of collective democratic determinations was championed by political philosopher Thomas Hobbes in his Leviathan (1651). He argued strongly against the "disease" of democracy, which would allow for mob rule and create anarchy, and was an advocate for centralised leadership. By contrast, John Locke's Second Treatise on Government (1742) supported political democracy as a legitimate means of ensuring that the people were represented. In England, radical thinker Thomas Paine similarly supported democracy as being necessary to ensure that citizens are represented. The Founding Fathers of the United States were primarily interested in creating a limited republic based on property ownership and representation rather than a full-fledged democracy. Despite these ideological differences, there was widespread agreement across Europe and North America that democracy should be based on the principle of equality before the law (the concept of equal rights for all citizens).
